area: Area IV. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can tell when an approach is no longer stabilized, decide early to go around, and fly a go-around (power, attitude, configuration) to ACS standards while avoiding traffic and staying in control.
why: A go-around is a normal maneuver, not a failure [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. It only becomes dangerous when it is delayed or flown badly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]], and mismanaged energy is a factor in approach-and-landing accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

prereading.what: Wrong surface landing avoidance and the stabilized approach concept, including the stabilized approach criteria and the 500 ft / 300 ft go-around guidance.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 9, 9-4 to 9-6

prereading.what: Go-arounds (rejected landings): why pilots delay, power, attitude, configuration, ground effect, common errors.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 9, 9-10 to 9-12

prereading.what: Energy errors on final approach: when to use throttle, when to use elevator.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 4, 4-11 to 4-13

prereading.what: Faulty approaches and landings, and when each one calls for a go-around.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 9, 9-30 to 9-34

prereading.what: LAHSO pilot responsibilities, including a rejected landing after accepting LAHSO.
prereading.label: AIM 4-3-11

warmup: You're on short final, a bit fast, and the airplane is still floating halfway down the runway. What makes many pilots try to save the landing instead of going around? What would make you go around?

key_terms.def: A normal maneuver to stop an approach when things don't go as expected or it is hazardous to continue [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
A constant-angle glide path to a chosen point on the runway, at a constant final descent airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
The spot your glide path would hit with no flare; it seems to stay still in the windshield [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].
Believing things are less threatening than they are and that the approach is sure to end in a safe landing [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Planning, monitoring and controlling altitude and airspeed targets [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].
Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature; the airplane performs as if it were at that altitude [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]].
Lower induced drag near the ground; "borrowed" performance you give back as you climb out of it [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
A stall caused by adding full power for a go-around with nose-up approach trim and not holding the nose down [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
VX: most altitude per distance over the ground. VY: most altitude per unit of time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Land and Hold Short Operations: landing and holding short of an intersecting runway, taxiway or other point [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]].
Any occurrence on the runway environment involving an aircraft, vehicle, person or object that creates a collision hazard or loss of separation [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]].

chunks.title: The stabilized approach and your energy

body.p: A stabilized approach is a constant-angle glide path to a chosen point on the runway, flown at a constant airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. The aiming point does not move in the windshield, and the runway shape stays the same, just bigger [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].
For a typical piston airplane, the AFH lists these stabilized approach criteria [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]:

head: Item
Stabilized means
rows: Glide path
Typically a constant 3 degrees to the touchdown zone (obstructions permitting)
Heading
Tracking the centerline with only minor corrections; bank normally limited to 15 degrees on final
Airspeed
Within +10/-5 KIAS of the recommended landing speed (AFM, 1.3 VSO, or placards)
Configuration
Landing configuration, flaps as required, gear down, in trim
Descent rate
Generally 500-1000 fpm; if over 500 fpm, reduce it before 300 ft AGL
Power
Appropriate for the configuration, not below the AFM minimum for approach
Briefings/checklists
Done before the approach (except the landing checklist)

callout.text: Go-around gates: not stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation in VMC (1,000 ft in IMC) - go around. In the pattern, if it becomes unstabilized below 300 ft AGL - go around now [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: Think of altitude and airspeed as stored energy. Throttle changes your total energy; elevator trades energy between altitude and airspeed [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].

bullets: Low AND slow (too little total energy): add power [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].
Low but fast (energy in the wrong place): ease back on the elevator to trade speed for altitude [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].
Low on glide path but on speed: add power AND ease back together [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].
Very slow: even full power may not be enough. You must lower the nose first to cut drag, which costs altitude. Too close to the ground, there may be no room to recover [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].

callout.text: Never stretch a glide with pitch alone. Raising the nose without power slows you down and can cause a high sink rate or a low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

check.q: You're in the pattern at 250 ft AGL and the approach becomes unstabilized. What does the AFH recommend?
check.a: An immediate go-around; the AFH says to go around if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 ft AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

chunks.title: When to go around, and why pilots wait too long

body.p: Reasons to go around include ATC instructions, a hazard on the runway, overtaking another airplane, wind shear, wake turbulence, a mechanical problem, or an unstable approach [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. Any approach may end in a go-around; it does not mean you flew badly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
The AFH also calls for a go-around in these landing problems:

head: What you see
AFH guidance
rows: Too slow and too low on final
Best to go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Sink rate excessive on a high approach (more than 800-1,000 fpm is excessive)
Go around [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
High round out; nose must be lowered a lot, or landing uncertain
Go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Floating: can't land in the first third, or drifting sideways
Go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
Excessive balloon
Go around immediately; add power before a stall [[24:204|AFH 9-33]]
Severe bounce
Go around immediately; don't try to save it [[24:205|AFH 9-34]]
Unsure you're lined up with the right runway
Go around [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]
Traffic on the runway may not clear in time
Go around early [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]

body.p: The most critical go-around is the one started very close to the ground. The maneuver itself isn't dangerous; it becomes dangerous only when delayed or flown badly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Delay comes from two traps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]:

bullets: Landing expectancy (set): believing the approach is sure to end in a safe landing.
Pride: thinking a go-around admits failure.

callout.text: Decide before you need to. Brief yourself on short final: "If I'm not stabilized at my gate, or not down in the first third, I go around." Indecision and delay are both listed common errors [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

check.q: Name the two sources of delay in starting a go-around.

chunks.title: Wind, density altitude and climb performance

body.p: Thin air (high density altitude) cuts three things you need in a go-around [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]]:

bullets: Power - the engine takes in less air.
Thrust - the propeller is less efficient.
Lift - thin air exerts less force on the wings.

body.p: High density altitude comes from high elevation, low pressure, high temperature and high humidity [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]]. Climb performance also drops with more weight, higher altitude, gear down and flaps down, because each cuts excess power [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. In a go-around you start with flaps and gear down, so expect a weak climb until you clean up.

callout.text: Ground effect is borrowed performance. Near the ground it helps you stop the descent, but climbing out too early can leave you unable to climb or even hold altitude at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

body.p: Wind matters too:

bullets: Wind changes your glide distance over the ground; correct with pitch and power [[24:174|AFH 9-3]].
Gusty air: many pilots add half the gust factor. Example: normal 70 knots, gusts of 15 knots, fly 77 knots [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Follow the POH.
Wind shear: a decreasing headwind lowers airspeed and lift and increases sink. A stabilized approach helps you spot the trend early [[28:272|AWH 22-17]].

Go around at the first sign of a microburst; some can't be escaped at low altitude [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. If caught, the AWH says hold or raise pitch and accept a lower airspeed instead of lowering the nose to regain speed [[28:268|AWH 22-13]]. Your airplane's technique comes from the POH/AFM and your CFI.
Wake turbulence is a reason to go around [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. After a larger airplane makes a low approach or missed approach, wait at least 2 minutes before landing [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

check.q: On a hot day at a high-elevation airport, what three things does the thin air reduce?
check.a: Engine power, propeller thrust, and wing lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]].

chunks.title: Wind correction on approach and climb-out

body.p: On approach, use the crab or the wing-low (sideslip) method. The wing-low method is recommended in most cases, but learn both [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

head: Method
How
Note
rows: Crab
Turn the nose into the wind so the ground track follows the centerline [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]
Must remove the crab with rudder just before touchdown [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]
Wing-low (sideslip)
Rudder lines the nose up with the runway; aileron lowers the upwind wing just enough to stop drift [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]
Axis and track stay aligned all the way to touchdown [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]

body.p: If full opposite rudder can't stop the turn in a wing-low approach, the wind is too strong for that runway. Use a better runway or another airport [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
On takeoff and climb-out, the same wind keeps pushing you [[24:140|AFH 6-8]]:

bullets: Once airborne, the airplane drifts with the wind; it can sideslip at first.
As the climb is set, turn the nose into the wind (crab), level the wings, and use rudder to stay over the runway and its extended centerline.
Wind can change a lot within a few hundred feet of the ground, so check your ground track often and adjust the crab.

callout.text: In a go-around, you go from a wing-low approach to a climb. Keep the upwind wing correction while the airplane is still low and slow, then transition to a crab as you climb, the same way you would after a crosswind takeoff [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

check.q: During the climb-out after a go-around in a crosswind, how do you stay over the extended centerline?
check.a: Turn the nose into the wind (crab), wings level, rudder as needed, and check ground track often because wind changes near the ground [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

body.p: Three cardinal principles, in order: Power, Attitude, Configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Your POH procedure, speeds and flap settings come first; the AFH is generic [[24:172|AFH 9-1]].

bullets: 1. Decide. Make a timely decision to go around [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
2. POWER. Full (or max allowable) takeoff power, smoothly and without hesitation. Carburetor heat off, as applicable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
3. ATTITUDE. Expect the nose to rise and yaw left. Hold forward elevator pressure to keep the nose level or in a safe climb attitude; add right rudder [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
4. Don't pitch up without airspeed. If slow, lower the nose briefly to gain speed; a few moments of level flight may be needed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].
5. CONFIGURATION. Once the descent is stopped, partially retract flaps (or to the takeoff setting per the manufacturer) [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
6. Climb at VY (VX if you must clear an obstacle) [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:271|AFH 13-22]] [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. Rough trim to relieve control pressure [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
7. Positive rate of climb confirmed: retract the gear, if retractable [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
8. Retract the remaining flaps in small steps as you accelerate [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
9. If the go-around is for traffic, move to the side so you can keep it in sight [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].
10. Fly the upwind leg; when at a safe altitude, a shallow turn to the upwind side helps you see departing traffic [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].
11. Radio: tell the tower, or announce on CTAF [[24:168|AFH 8-4]] [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].
12. Checklist: review the go-around (balked landing) checklist as workload permits, then re-do the full before-landing checklist before the next approach [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].

body.p: ACS tolerances for this Task:

head: Item
Standard
rows: Power and pitch
Apply takeoff power immediately and transition to climb pitch attitude for VX or VY as appropriate, +10/-5 knots (ACS PA.IV.N.S4)
Climb
Maintain VY +10/-5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude (ACS PA.IV.N.S7)
Configuration
Configure after a positive rate of climb is verified, or per the manufacturer (ACS PA.IV.N.S5)
Track
Maintain directional control and wind-drift correction throughout the climb (ACS PA.IV.N.S8)

callout.text: "Power - Attitude - Configuration." Cram, climb, clean up. Flaps before gear [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
If the wheels touch during a very low go-around, that's OK. Keep it straight, hold a constant safe pitch, and keep the power in [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

check.q: Why retract flaps (at least partially) before the landing gear?
check.a: Full flaps usually make more drag than the gear, and you want the gear down and locked if the airplane touches down as the go-around starts [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

body.p: The AFH lists these go-around errors [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]:

head: Error
Fix
rows: Not recognizing a condition that warrants a go-around
Know your gates: stabilized by 500 ft (VMC), go around if unstable below 300 ft [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Indecision / delay in starting
Decide early; a go-around is normal [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]
Not applying max allowable power in time
Power is your first concern [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Abrupt power application
Smooth and positive; abrupt throttle can make some engines falter [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Improper pitch attitude
Forward pressure, then rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Not configuring properly
Flaps in steps after descent stops; gear after positive climb [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Climbing out of ground effect too soon
Get flying speed first [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Not correcting for torque/P-factor
Right rudder with the power [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Loss of aircraft control
Fly the airplane first; control comes before reaching for the flap handle [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]

callout.text: The gear-up trap: a go-around breaks your habit pattern. Re-do the whole before-landing checklist before the next landing [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].

check.q: What can happen if you jam the throttle forward abruptly?
check.a: In some airplanes the engine may falter; power should be smooth and positive [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

chunks.title: Risk: power, pitch, flaps and losing control down low

body.p: At go-around time you are trimmed nose-up for a slow approach. Full power adds propwash over the tail, and the nose rises sharply and turns left [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. If you let it, you get an elevator trim stall, possibly unrecoverable that low [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

bullets: Power (R3): full power, smooth and without hesitation, held until flying speed and control are restored [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Pitch: an airplane can't fly below stall speed and can't climb below minimum power required speed. Resist pitching up if airspeed is low [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Configuring (R4): a sudden, complete flap retraction can make you lose lift and settle into the ground. Retract in small steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

Expect quick pitch-force changes as flaps come up, because of the trim setting and higher airflow. Use the same flap settings at the same pattern points so the go-around is familiar [[24:235|AFH 12-4]] [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].
Don't retract flaps to fix a low approach; it causes a sudden loss of lift and more sink [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

body.p: Low-altitude stall/spin (R6): overshooting the turn to final and fixing it with more bank, back pressure and inside rudder sets up a cross-control stall that can quickly become a spin. The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around. Down low, be reluctant to bank more than 30 degrees, and never skid to fix an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

CFIT and energy (R6): energy mismanagement contributes to loss of control, CFIT, and approach-and-landing accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. If you're very slow and near the ground, there may not be room to recover [[24:99|AFH 4-13]]. Go around early, while you still have energy.

callout.text: Airplane control is the first consideration in this high-workload phase [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

check.q: You add full power with nose-up trim. Which way does the nose go, and what do you do?
check.a: It pitches up and yaws left. Hold firm forward elevator pressure, add right rudder, then rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

chunks.title: Risk: traffic, runways, LAHSO and distractions

body.p: Collision hazards (R5, S6):

bullets: If you go around for traffic on the ground or in the air, move to the side to keep it in sight; this may mean a slight offset from the runway [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].
If the turn to final would create a collision hazard, or you'd be overtaking someone, go around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].
High wings block your view above; low wings block the view below. Bank now and then to uncover blind spots [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].
Unless ATC says otherwise, a VFR go-around overflies the runway, climbs to pattern altitude and enters via the crosswind leg [[34:353|AIM P/CG]].

body.p: Runway incursion (R8, S9): a runway incursion is any event on the runway involving an aircraft, vehicle, person or object that creates a collision hazard or loss of separation with an airplane landing or taking off [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]]. On final, verify the runway number and alignment; if in doubt about the landing surface, go around [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. Traffic on the runway that may not clear in time is a reason for an early go-around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].
LAHSO (R9): student pilots or pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. You'll still meet it as a private pilot, so know the rules:

bullets: The PIC can accept or decline. Decline if it compromises safety [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].
A LAHSO clearance does not prevent a rejected landing [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

If you reject the landing, keep safe separation from other aircraft and vehicles and promptly notify the controller [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]]. Remember someone may be crossing or landing on the other runway.

body.p: Distractions and workload (R7): approach and landing is a high-workload time. When task saturated, a pilot may fixate on one item and miss others [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Fly first, then talk. Use a sterile flight deck during arrival [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

callout.text: Radio (S2): at a towered airport, ATC may say "Go around" [[34:353|AIM P/CG]]; if you go around on your own, tell the controller [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. At a non-towered airport, communicate your position on CTAF to avoid a traffic conflict [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].

check.q: You accepted LAHSO and must reject the landing. What two things does the AIM say to do?
check.a: Maintain safe separation from other aircraft and vehicles, and promptly notify the controller [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

f1.caption: Figure 9-12. Go-around procedure.
f1.alt: Twin airplane sequence over a runway: timely decision to make go-around; apply max power, adjust pitch attitude, allow airspeed to increase; assume climb attitude, flaps to intermediate; positive rate of climb, retract gear, climb at VY; retract remaining flaps; 500 feet cruise climb.

f2.caption: Figure 9-5. Stabilized approach.
f2.alt: A high-wing airplane descends on a straight blue glide path toward an aiming point near the runway threshold, then flares and touches down farther along; the distance traveled in flare is marked.

f3.caption: Figure 4-13. Energy error management.
f3.alt: Airplane below the desired glideslope, and a circle chart of altitude (high/low) versus airspeed (slow/fast): total energy errors are corrected with throttle, energy distribution errors with elevator; points B, C and D show low-and-slow, low-on-speed, and low-and-fast.

f4.caption: Figure 5-14. Elevator trim stall.
f4.alt: Airplane sequence: configured for landing and trimmed nose-up; maximum power applied for a simulated go-around lets the nose rise; before a full stall the pilot applies forward pressure, eliminates the stall warning and re-trims; return to the desired flightpath.

f5.caption: Figure 9-17. Crosswind approach and landing.
f5.alt: A high-wing airplane flies a wing-low approach down a straight path to the runway with a crosswind arrow and windsock, touching down on the upwind main wheel and rolling out on the centerline.

f6.caption: AIM FIG 4-3-8. Land and Hold Short of an Intersecting Runway.
f6.alt: Diagram of two intersecting runways: one aircraft cleared to land using the full length of its runway, the other cleared to land and hold short, with red 27-9 hold-short signs and markings before the intersection.

scenario.title: Busy Class D, hot afternoon, a plane on the runway
scenario.setup: You're a new private pilot landing at a towered airport with crossing runways on a hot, gusty afternoon. You're trimmed for approach with full flaps. The tower offers you a land and hold short clearance. On a 1-mile final you're a bit high and fast, and your passenger is asking about dinner plans. At about 200 ft AGL you see a small airplane taxiing onto your runway.

questions.q: Should you accept the LAHSO clearance?
questions.a: Only if you know the available landing distance and your airplane can land and stop within it [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]; the PIC may decline [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Student pilots and pilots unfamiliar with LAHSO should not participate [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Declining is a fine choice.

questions.q: You're high and fast at 600 ft AGL. What should you be thinking?
questions.a: Use power and pitch to get stabilized now. If not stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation, go around; below 300 ft, an unstabilized approach means an immediate go-around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Don't dive at the runway: a sink rate over 800-1,000 fpm is excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

questions.q: How do you handle the chatty passenger?
questions.a: Ask for a sterile flight deck during arrival [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. Distractions and task saturation make pilots fixate and miss things [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

questions.q: The airplane pulls onto your runway at 200 ft. What do you do first?
questions.a: Go around now. Full power smoothly, forward pressure against the nose-up trim, right rudder [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Don't wait to see if it clears; landing expectancy causes deadly delays [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

questions.q: It's hot and gusty, and you have full flaps. What do you expect, and how do you clean up?
questions.a: Weak climb: high density altitude cuts power, thrust and lift, and flaps cut excess power [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]] [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. Stop the descent, then retract flaps in small steps; don't climb out of ground effect too soon [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

questions.q: Where do you fly, and what do you say?
questions.a: Offset slightly to the side to keep the airplane on the runway in sight [[24:272|AFH 13-23]], and tell the tower you're going around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. If you had accepted LAHSO, also keep separation from traffic on the crossing runway and promptly notify the controller [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

questions.q: Back on downwind, what must you not forget?
questions.a: Re-do the entire before-landing checklist; a go-around is a classic setup for a gear-up landing [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].

skills.do: Complete the appropriate checklists: the go-around (balked landing) checklist, then the before-landing checklist again.
skills.practice: Do the go-around from memory first, then review the checklist when workload allows [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].
Script calls: tell the tower you're going around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]], or announce your position on CTAF [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]]. Fly first, then talk.

skills.do: Decide in time to discontinue the approach.
skills.practice: Set gates: stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation (VMC); unstabilized below 300 ft AGL means go around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Have your CFI call surprise go-arounds.

skills.do: Apply takeoff power immediately and transition to climb pitch for VX or VY as appropriate, +10/-5 knots (ACS PA.IV.N.S4).
skills.practice: Smooth full power, forward pressure, right rudder, then pitch for the climb [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Learn the climb attitude against the horizon.

skills.do: Configure the airplane after a positive rate of climb is verified, or per the manufacturer.
skills.practice: Flaps in steps once the descent stops; gear up after positive rate of climb [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

skills.do: Move to the side of the runway when needed to clear and avoid conflicting traffic.
skills.practice: Practice a slight offset so the traffic stays in view [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].

skills.do: Maintain VY +10/-5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude (ACS PA.IV.N.S7).
skills.practice: Rough trim early, then fine trim once stable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

skills.do: Keep directional control and wind-drift correction throughout the climb.
skills.practice: Crab into the wind over the extended centerline and check ground track often [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

skills.do: Use runway incursion avoidance procedures, if applicable.
skills.practice: Verify runway number and alignment on every final; go around if in doubt [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. Watch for traffic entering the runway [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

quiz.q: The three cardinal principles of a go-around, in order, are:
options: Configuration, power, attitude
Power, attitude, configuration
Attitude, configuration, power
Power, configuration, attitude

quiz.q: In VMC, a pilot should typically go around if not stabilized by:
options: 300 ft above airport elevation
500 ft above airport elevation
1,000 ft above airport elevation
Short final
quiz.why: 500 ft above airport elevation in VMC (1,000 ft in IMC) [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

quiz.q: In the traffic pattern, the AFH says to go around immediately if the approach becomes unstabilized below:
options: 300 ft AGL
100 ft AGL
500 ft AGL
800 ft AGL
quiz.why: Below 300 ft AGL, an unstabilized approach calls for an immediate go-around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

quiz.q: You add full power with the airplane trimmed for the approach. You should expect:
options: The nose to drop and yaw right
The nose to rise and yaw left
No change in pitch
The nose to drop and yaw left
quiz.why: Sudden power raises the nose and causes left yaw; hold forward pressure and right rudder [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: Why should flaps come up in small increments during a go-around?
options: To protect the flap motor from overload while power is at maximum
To prevent the stall warning from sounding as the airplane accelerates
A sudden full retraction can cause a loss of lift and settling
Because the gear must be fully retracted before any flap movement starts
quiz.why: Retract in small steps so the airplane can accelerate; a sudden full retraction can make it settle [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: Unless the POH says otherwise, which comes up first?
options: Flaps (at least partially), then gear after a positive rate of climb
Landing gear first, because it normally makes more drag than the flaps
Both at the same time, as soon as full power is set on the engine
Neither one until you have climbed back up to pattern altitude
quiz.why: Full flaps usually make more drag than the gear, and the gear should be down if you touch the runway [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

quiz.q: You go around because of an airplane on the runway. The AFH suggests you:
options: Climb steeply straight over it
Turn crosswind immediately at low altitude
Maneuver to the side to keep it in sight
Reduce power to stay behind it
quiz.why: Consider maneuvering to the side to keep the conflicting traffic in sight [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].

quiz.q: After accepting a LAHSO clearance, you must reject the landing. The AIM says:
options: You may not reject the landing once you have accepted the clearance
Maintain safe separation and promptly notify the controller
Hold short anyway and request a new clearance from the controller
Continue and land long on the crossing runway if it appears clear
quiz.why: LAHSO does not preclude a rejected landing; keep safe separation and promptly notify the controller [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

takeaways: A go-around is a normal maneuver; landing expectancy and pride cause deadly delays.
Stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation (VMC); go around if unstabilized below 300 ft AGL.
Power, attitude, configuration: full power, forward pressure and right rudder, then flaps in steps and gear after a positive climb.
Ground effect and high density altitude can hide a weak climb; get flying speed first.
Hold VY +10/-5 knots, keep wind correction, and offset to keep traffic in sight.
Tell ATC or announce on CTAF, then re-do the before-landing checklist.
cfi_notes: Call surprise go-arounds at different heights, including from the round out and a bounce; the AFH says low-airspeed go-arounds may need a few moments of level flight to accelerate [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].
Demo the elevator trim stall tendency at altitude so the student feels how much forward pressure full power needs [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Watch for students grabbing the flap handle before the airplane is under control [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Teach go-arounds as normal from the first landing lesson; the AFH calls the poor-approach stigma a fallacy [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Use the same flap settings at the same pattern points so the go-around sequence is familiar [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].
Examiners probe the stabilized approach criteria, why flaps come before gear, and LAHSO rules for students.
The Task S4 text appears garbled in the source ('V or V ... X Y'); it means VX or VY +10/-5 knots.
gaps: Airplane-specific go-around procedure, speeds (VX, VY, approach speed), flap retraction steps and power settings come from the POH/AFM.
None of these sources gives standard CTAF phraseology for a go-around; only the general self-announce guidance (AIM 4-1-9) is used.
The sources don't directly explain how headwind or tailwind change the go-around climb angle over the ground.

FAA cancelled AC 00-54 (Pilot Windshear Guide) in 2022; wind shear guidance now sits in the Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28B). The AWH covers recognition, going around at the first sign, and the general rule to hold pitch and accept lower airspeed [[28:268|AWH 22-13]], but its encounter studies are airline-style (crews, thrust, stick shaker) and it gives no step-by-step windshear escape or go-around procedure for small airplanes. Use the POH/AFM and your CFI.

activities.title: Throttle, elevator, or both?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Below the glide path and slower than target
Above the glide path and faster than target
Below the glide path and faster than target
Above the glide path and slower than target
Below the glide path, right on target speed
Climb back to the path without changing airspeed

activities.title: True or false: go around or keep going?

cards.s: You are floating and can't touch down in the first third of the runway. You should go around.
cards.why: Yes. If you can't land on the first third of the runway, or the airplane drifts sideways, go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].

cards.s: After a severe bounce, the best move is to flare again and save the landing.
cards.why: No. After a severe bounce, the safest procedure is to go around immediately. Don't try to salvage the landing [[24:205|AFH 9-34]].

cards.s: A go-around means your approach was poor and you lack skill.
cards.why: No. Any approach may end in a go-around. The AFH calls that idea a fallacy [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

cards.s: Diving at the runway on a high final at 1,200 feet per minute is fine if you stay on the centerline.
cards.why: No. A sink rate over 800-1,000 fpm is excessive. Go around if the sink rate becomes excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

cards.s: If you are unsure you are lined up with the right runway, you should go around.
cards.why: Yes. If there is doubt about the landing surface, go around and think it over [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

cards.s: If you are too slow and too low on final, the AFH says it is best to go around.
cards.why: Yes. Too slow and too low: it is best to go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

activities.title: Fly the go-around in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Decide to go around, without delay
Add full power smoothly; carb heat off, if applicable
Hold forward pressure and right rudder as the nose rises
Descent stopped: raise the flaps partway (or to takeoff setting)
Positive rate of climb: retract the gear, if retractable
Raise the rest of the flaps in small steps as you speed up
Before the next landing, re-do the whole before-landing checklist

activities.title: What can that mistake do?
activities.intro: Tap a mistake, then what it can lead to.

pairs.r: Nose rises sharply and turns left; risk of a stall
Sudden loss of lift; the airplane settles toward the ground

pairs.l: Climbing out of ground effect early
pairs.r: May not climb, or even hold altitude, at full power
In some airplanes, the engine may falter

pairs.l: No before-landing checklist after a go-around
pairs.r: A gear-up landing on the next approach

pairs.l: Skidding turn to fix an overshoot
pairs.r: Cross-control stall that can quickly become a spin

final_quiz.q: Your POH recommended landing speed is 65 KIAS. Using the AFH stabilized approach criteria, which airspeed on final means you are NOT stabilized?
options: 73 KIAS
61 KIAS
74 KIAS
58 KIAS
final_quiz.why: Stabilized means within +10/-5 KIAS of the recommended landing speed: 65 - 5 = 60 and 65 + 10 = 75 KIAS. 58 KIAS is below 60 [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: You are landing in VMC at an airport with a field elevation of 1,200 feet MSL. By what altimeter reading should you be stabilized, or else go around?
options: 1,500 feet MSL
2,200 feet MSL
1,700 feet MSL
500 feet MSL
final_quiz.why: The gate is 500 feet above airport elevation in VMC: 1,200 + 500 = 1,700 feet MSL. 2,200 would be the 1,000-foot IMC gate [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: On final you are below the glide path, and your airspeed is 10 knots above target. What is the best correction?
options: Ease back on the elevator to trade the extra speed for altitude
Add power and leave the pitch alone
Lower the nose and reduce power
Raise one notch of flaps
final_quiz.why: Low and fast is an energy distribution error. You have enough total energy, so use the elevator to trade speed for altitude [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]. Raising flaps to fix an undershoot can cause a sudden loss of lift [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: To clear trees on a steep final, you are descending at 800 feet per minute. According to the AFH stabilized approach criteria, what is the latest point to reduce the descent rate?
options: Before the round out
Before 500 feet AGL
Before 1,000 feet AGL
Before 300 feet AGL
final_quiz.why: If you use a descent rate over 500 fpm, reduce it before 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: You are floating past the first third of the runway. You think, "This always works out. I'll get it down." Which hazard is this?
options: Pride
Landing expectancy (set)
Task saturation
Complacency about the checklist
final_quiz.why: Landing expectancy is the belief that things are not as threatening as they are and that the approach is sure to end in a safe landing [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Pride is thinking a go-around admits failure. You should go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].

final_quiz.q: In which situation should you expect the weakest climb in a go-around?
options: Sea-level airport, cool dry day, flaps up, light load
Sea-level airport, cool day, full flaps, light load
High-elevation airport, cold dry day, flaps up, light load
High elevation, hot humid day, full flaps, heavy load
final_quiz.why: High elevation, heat and humidity all raise density altitude, which cuts power, thrust and lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]]. More weight and lowered flaps also reduce climb performance [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].

final_quiz.q: You go around from just above the runway. The airplane feels like it is floating on a cushion of air, so you pull up into a steep climb right away. What is the risk?
options: The engine may overheat from running high power for so long at low airspeed
The stall speed drops in a steep pitch-up, so there is no risk of a stall
The flaps may be damaged by the higher airspeed as the airplane accelerates
The airplane may not climb, or even hold altitude, outside ground effect
final_quiz.why: Ground effect lowers induced drag. That borrowed performance is repaid as you climb out of it, and an early climb may leave you unable to climb or hold altitude at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: During the climb after a go-around, the wind is from the right. How do you stay over the runway's extended centerline?
options: Turn the nose right into the wind, wings level, and check the ground track
Keep the right wing low with the nose straight all the way to pattern altitude
Let the airplane drift for now and correct it once on the crosswind leg
Turn the nose left of runway heading, wings level, and hold that heading
final_quiz.why: As the climb is set, turn the nose into the wind (crab), level the wings, and use rudder to stay over the runway and its extended centerline. Wind can change within a few hundred feet, so check the ground track often [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

final_quiz.q: You start a go-around from the round out, with the airspeed well below normal approach speed. After adding full power, what should you do with pitch?
options: Hold the nose level or near level briefly while the airplane speeds up
Pitch up right away to the VY attitude to get the best climb rate
Raise the flaps all the way up first, then pitch up once they are retracted
Pitch up to the VX attitude right away, since you are so close to the ground
final_quiz.why: Don't pitch up for a climb without enough airspeed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. From a low airspeed, the first priority is control and flying speed. A few moments of level or near level flight may be needed [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].

final_quiz.q: During a very low go-around, the main wheels touch the runway once after you add power. What should you do?
options: Close the throttle and land, since your wheels are already on the runway
Keep it straight, hold a constant safe pitch, and keep the power in
Pull back hard on the yoke to get airborne again before another bounce
Raise all the flaps at once to cut drag and let the airplane gain speed
final_quiz.why: Settling onto the runway in a very low go-around is not particularly dangerous if you keep the airplane straight and hold a constant, safe pitch. The power quickly brings flying speed [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Continue the go-around even if another bounce happens [[24:205|AFH 9-34]].

final_quiz.q: You are flying VFR on final at a towered airport. The tower says, "Go around," with no other instructions. What should you do?
options: Turn crosswind right away, before the runway end, to get off the runway path
Level off and circle left at your current altitude until the tower calls you
Fly the published missed approach procedure for the runway you were landing on
Overfly the runway, climb to pattern altitude, and enter via crosswind
final_quiz.why: Unless ATC says otherwise, a VFR aircraft overflies the runway while climbing to traffic pattern altitude and enters the pattern via the crosswind leg. The published missed approach is for IFR pilots on an instrument approach [[34:353|AIM P/CG]].

final_quiz.q: You are a student pilot on a solo flight. The tower offers you a land and hold short clearance. What does the AIM say?
options: Accept it; the tower would not offer it if it were not safe for you
Accept it, then reject the landing if you find you cannot hold short
Student pilots should not take part in LAHSO, so decline it
Accept it only if the wind is calm and the runway is dry and clear
final_quiz.why: Student pilots or pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate. The PIC has final authority to accept or decline [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

final_quiz.q: In a left pattern, you overshoot the centerline turning base to final. You are tempted to steepen the bank, pull back, and add left rudder to get lined up. What is the safest action?
options: Steepen the bank to 45 degrees
Add more left rudder to skid the nose around
Go around
Hold the bank and pull back harder
final_quiz.why: Those inputs set up a cross-control stall that can quickly become a spin. The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around. Down low, avoid banks over 30 degrees and never skid to fix an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
